column2: Indicate the expected amount of time required to complete the lesson or learning experience. This helps with lesson pacing and planning, and may refer to a single session or span multiple periods depending on the activity scope.

Describe the overarching type or focus of inquiry guiding the lesson (e.g., factual, conceptual, or debatable). This should highlight how students will engage with content—whether by gathering information, exploring big ideas, or considering multiple perspectives.
List specific questions designed to uncover concrete facts or recall information. These questions typically have clear, right-or-wrong answers and help students build foundational knowledge.
Include open-ended questions that explore broader ideas, patterns, or relationships. These questions promote deeper understanding and transfer of learning across contexts.
Present complex, open-ended questions that have multiple valid answers or viewpoints. These questions encourage critical thinking, discussion, and evidence-based reasoning.

Identify the student behaviors or dispositions that will be emphasized or developed during the lesson. These might include collaboration, persistence, critical thinking, risk-taking, or reflective thinking, and often align with learner profiles or capabilities frameworks.

Explain how teaching and learning will be adjusted to meet the varied needs, interests, and abilities of students. This may include scaffolds, extensions, varied groupings, choice-based tasks, or adapted assessments to ensure all learners are supported and challenged.
